title: Why Your House Doesn't Fall Down
blurb: Every wall, beam and roof in your house is doing a job. Here is how a house holds itself up, keeps the weather out, and why houses look different everywhere.

blocks.prompt: How a House Gets Built
blocks.text: A house starts as a hole in the ground. Workers fill the hole with concrete. That is the foundation. It holds the whole house up. Next come the walls. Inside the walls are long pieces of wood called studs. They stand in a row like a fence. Then the roof goes on. The roof is built out of triangles. Triangles are strong. You can push on a triangle and it will not bend. Last of all come the windows and the door. Now the house can keep the rain out and keep you warm.

blocks.prompt: Passing the Weight Along
blocks.text: Stand in any room and look up. The roof over your head is heavy. So is the snow or the rain that lands on it. So why does none of it come down on you? The answer is that a house passes weight along, hand to hand, all the way to the ground. It starts at the roof. The roof rests on rafters, which are long slanted beams. The rafters push their load onto the walls. Inside every wall is a row of upright wooden posts called studs, standing about sixteen inches apart. Studs are good at one job: holding weight straight down. The studs pass the load to the foundation, a thick slab or wall of concrete under the whole house. The foundation is wide, so it spreads the weight over a big patch of soil. The soil holds. Builders call this the load path. If any part of the path is missing, the house sags. That is why you cannot just cut a hole anywhere you like in a wall. Some walls are only dividers. Others are holding the house up.

4.title: Why Your House Doesn't Fall Down
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: Why Your House Doesn't Fall Down

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Heat only moves from warm toward cold
Insulation is really just trapped air
Snow is mostly air, so an igloo holds heat
Adobe walls run about half a day behind the sun
Your heater replaces heat, it does not store it

blocks.prompt: A House Is a Trap for Air
blocks.text: A house has one job that has nothing to do with holding itself up. It has to keep the weather on the outside and keep you comfortable on the inside. Heat is stubborn about this. Heat always moves from warm places toward cold ones, and it never moves the other way on its own. In winter, the heat inside your house is constantly leaking out through the walls, the roof, and the glass. Your heater is not really making a warm house. It is replacing what the house loses. So builders slow the leak down. The trick is air. Still air is a terrible conductor of heat, so if you can trap air and stop it from moving, you have a barrier. That is all insulation is: a material full of tiny pockets of trapped air. Fluffy pink fiberglass, foam board, sheep wool, even shredded newspaper all work the same way. The material barely matters. The trapped air does the work. People figured this out long before anyone used the word insulation. An igloo is built from blocks of packed snow, which is mostly air, and a person inside can sit forty degrees Fahrenheit warmer than the night outdoors. In hot, dry places, people built with adobe: mud bricks a foot thick. Thick earth walls take most of a day for heat to cross, so the house stays cool while the sun is up, then gives that stored heat back after dark, exactly when it is wanted. Neither builder had a physics textbook. Both had noticed something true about heat and built a house around it.

5.title: Why Your House Doesn't Fall Down
5.subtitle: A reading and history sheet for ages 11 to 12

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Catalhoyuk, Turkey: houses entered through the roof
That town had no streets at all

blocks.prompt: The Rooms We Had to Invent
blocks.text: A house looks like an obvious idea, but almost every part of it had to be invented, and some of the inventions took thousands of years. Start with the wall. Around nine thousand years ago, in what is now Turkey, several thousand people lived in a town called Catalhoyuk. Their houses were built of mud brick and packed so tightly together that there were no streets at all. There were no front doors either. You reached your house by walking across the rooftops of your neighbors and climbing down a ladder through a hole in your own roof. The same hole let the smoke out. Nobody had thought of a chimney yet. The chimney is a surprisingly late idea. For most of human history, a fire burned in the middle of the room and the smoke found its own way out through the thatch, a vent, or your lungs. Medieval halls were black with soot. The chimney only became common in Europe about eight hundred years ago, and it changed the shape of the house immediately. Once smoke could be aimed at a flue, the fire could be pushed against a wall. Once the fire was against a wall, you could build a floor above it without filling the upstairs with smoke. The chimney is the reason houses have upstairs bedrooms. Windows were slower still. For centuries a window was simply a hole. You could cover it with a shutter, a stretched animal skin, or a piece of oiled cloth, and each of those choices was the same trade: light or warmth, pick one. Clear glass in a window was a Roman luxury, then largely forgotten in northern Europe, then a mark of wealth so plain that English houses were once taxed on how many windows they had. Owners bricked their windows up to lower the bill. You can still see the blank shapes in old English walls. Every ordinary thing in your house is like this. Someone lived without it, wanted it, and worked out how.

6.title: Why Your House Doesn't Fall Down
6.subtitle: A reading and analysis sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: Why Your House Doesn't Fall Down

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Thatch sheds water only above about 45 degrees of pitch
Flat roofs belong to dry places
Thick earth walls lag the sun by about 12 hours
Mesa Verde alcoves face south on purpose
A Mongolian ger packs up and travels
Air conditioning let builders stop listening to the site

blocks.prompt: The House Is an Argument With the Weather
blocks.text: For most of history, you could tell where you were by looking at the houses. Not because of decoration, but because a house was an argument with the local weather, made out of whatever was lying nearby, and the weather and the materials were different everywhere. Consider the roof. A roof made of thatch, which is bundled reed or straw, only sheds water if it is steep. Below roughly forty five degrees, water soaks in instead of running off, and the roof rots. So in the wet parts of northern Europe, where reed grew in the marshes, roofs climbed at sharp angles. Travel to the dry parts of the American Southwest or the Middle East and the roofs go flat, because there is almost nothing to shed, and a flat roof is cheaper, easier, and doubles as a place to sleep on a hot night. The roof is not a style choice. It is a reading of the rainfall. Consider the walls. Where the swing between day and night temperature is brutal, people built thick: adobe, rammed earth, stone. A wall two feet of packed earth thick takes most of a day for heat to cross, so it hands you the afternoon's warmth in the evening and the night's coolness at noon. It is a battery for heat, running about twelve hours behind the sun. Where wood was plentiful and winters were long, people built thin walls instead and stuffed them with anything that trapped air. Consider the whole house. The Ancestral Puebloans built into south-facing cliff alcoves at Mesa Verde, and the geometry is not an accident. Winter sun sits low and reaches deep under the overhang, warming the stone all day. Summer sun sits high, and the same overhang throws the whole village into shade. That is a solar heating system built around seven hundred fifty years ago out of nothing but a well-chosen hole in a cliff. A Mongolian ger goes the other way and solves a different problem: it is felt stretched over a wooden lattice, warm enough for a steppe winter, and it comes apart and travels with the herds. Then, in the middle of the twentieth century, the argument mostly stopped. Cheap fuel, cheap electricity, air conditioning, and materials that could be trucked a thousand miles meant a builder no longer had to listen to the site. The same house could be dropped in Maine or Arizona, and a machine would fix the difference. It worked, in the sense that people were comfortable. It also meant the house had stopped thinking, and the fuel bill did the thinking instead. The interesting part is that the argument is coming back, and it is coming back with instruments. Builders who follow the passive design standards obsess over exactly what the Puebloans obsessed over: which way the glass faces, how far the roof overhangs, how tight the shell is, where the sun will be in February. They can now measure what earlier builders could only notice across generations. The old houses were right for reasons nobody could write down. The new ones aim at the same target with a spreadsheet. Both are doing the same thing. They are asking the weather a question and building the answer.
